hypothesis: If whorl breadths (equivalently conch diameters one revolution apart) expand by a factor r per whorl, the constant angle is alpha = arccot(ln r / 2 pi) (Thompson's own table: r = 1.5 -> 86.3 deg, 2.0 -> 83.7 deg, 2.5 -> 81.7 deg, 3.0 -> 80.1 deg, 3.5 -> 78.7 deg). The claim then predicts: Nautilus r about 3, alpha about 80 deg; for ordinary ammonoids and typically spiral gastropods alpha is usually between 80 and 85 deg (r between 1.72 and 3.00) and very seldom below 80 deg (r > 3.00).
pass_criterion: Pre-registered. (a) Nautilus pompilius: per specimen, the median whorl expansion rate WER (Korn's definition, (dm1/dm2)^2 over half a whorl, which equals the per-revolution diameter ratio r) over all measured post-embryonic stages; the median across specimens, converted to alpha, must lie in [78, 82] deg (r in 2.6-3.5). (b) Ammonoids: per species, the median WER over measured stages with conch diameter >= 5 mm (excluding the embryonic ammonitella), converted to alpha; at least 50% of species must have alpha in [80, 85] deg and at most 10% alpha < 80 deg. (c) Gastropods: per specimen (then averaged per species), the fitted per-revolution whorl expansion rate W from the Collins et al. 2021 helicospiral fits, converted to alpha the same way; at least 50% of species in [80, 85] deg and at most 10% below 80 deg. All three of (a), (b), (c) must hold for 'supports'.
fail_criterion: Pre-registered. 'refutes' if the Nautilus median alpha is outside [76, 84] deg, or if in either the ammonoid or the gastropod sample fewer than 40% of species fall in [80, 85] deg, or more than 20% fall below 80 deg. Anything between the pass and fail thresholds is 'mixed'. If the gastropod expansion parameter cannot be mapped to a per-revolution ratio from the dataset's documentation, part (c) is reported as not operationalizable and the verdict rests on (a) and (b) with a caveat.
interpretation: Thompson defines the constant angle through the per-whorl ratio of radii or whorl breadths, r = e^(2 pi cot alpha), and reads the angle off that ratio; the test therefore measures r and converts it with his own formula rather than fitting tangent angles to outlines. Modern 'whorl expansion rate' (Korn: WER = (dm1/dm2)^2 across half a whorl; Raup: W per revolution) is the same quantity for a planispiral shell. 'Ordinary ammonitoid shells' is operationalized as the species in a large published cross-section dataset (Devonian-Jurassic), 'typically spiral gastropods' as the 25 fossil and modern helicospiral species measured by Collins et al. 2021; neither sample was chosen by the tester. Deviation from the pre-registration: Collins et al. publish no per-revolution W (their W_e is a fitted rate of aperture-area increase), so r was computed directly from their raw digitised apertures (distance of the aperture centroid from the coiling axis at 180-degree steps, r = r[k+2]/r[k]), which is Thompson's own quantity; Nautilus r was likewise taken directly as dm[i]/dm[i-8] over the 45-degree stations rather than through WER.

method: fetch.py obtains the files (Dryad downloads sit behind a browser proof-of-work challenge; they were fetched with headless Chrome and checksummed) and writes derived tables (committed). analysis.py computes, per Nautilus specimen, the median of dm[i]/dm[i-8] over the 45-degree stations (one revolution; all stations are post-hatching, first dm 18-27 mm); per ammonoid species, the median of dm[n]/dm[n-1] over half-whorl stations with dm >= 5 mm; per gastropod specimen, the median of r[k+2]/r[k] where r is the perpendicular distance of each digitised aperture's centroid from the coiling axis (apertures 180 deg apart; replicate digitisations pooled), then the median per species. Each r is converted to alpha = arccot(ln r / 2 pi) and the pre-registered band fractions are evaluated.

measured.unit: degrees, median constant angle of Nautilus pompilius (r = 2.87 per revolution)

caveats: The verdict follows the pre-registered rule, which fails because only 32% of ammonoid species (threshold 40%) and 46% of gastropod species fall inside 80-85 deg. The failure is one-sided: no ammonoid and no gastropod species, and only 5% of Nautilus, fall below 80 deg, so 'very seldom less than 80 deg' is strongly supported; the typical ammonoid and gastropod sits at 85-86 deg (r 1.5-1.7), just above Thompson's upper bound rather than inside it.

The Nautilus part of the claim ('in the neighbourhood of 80 deg', 'about three times') is confirmed closely: median 80.5 deg, r = 2.87, with very low scatter across 93 specimens and three populations.

The ammonoid sample (Walton & Korn 2018) was assembled to study pachyconic and globular conchs and is 82% Palaeozoic; globular Palaeozoic goniatites have low expansion rates, so it is probably biased towards high alpha relative to the Mesozoic ammonites Thompson likely had in mind (the 3 Jurassic and 6 of 11 Permian species are in band).

The gastropod sample is 26 species dominated by four struthiolariid/turritellid species from New Zealand and Australia; species were weighted equally, but it is not a random sample of 'typically spiral' gastropods. r for gastropods was measured on digitised apertures in a single sectioned plane (centroid distance from the axis), which is noisier than CT-based cephalopod diameters.
Per-species r is a median over ontogeny; whorl expansion drifts during growth (see thompson1917-ch11-08), so an adult-only or juvenile-only convention would move alpha by a fraction of a degree.

Sensitivity (not pre-registered, computed in a side check): the ammonoid in-band fraction is 0.26 with no size threshold, 0.32 at dm >= 5 mm (pre-registered), 0.29 at dm >= 10 mm, 0.26 at dm >= 20 mm, and 0.33 using only each species' last measured revolution; the median alpha stays at 85.5-85.6 deg and the below-80 fraction at 0 throughout, so the verdict does not depend on the threshold.
